en: The traditional Filipino kalesa uses the wheel and axle simple machine to reduce friction and transport passengers.
The rough volcanic rocks of the Mayon Volcano hiking trail increase friction to help climbers avoid slipping.
The fast-flowing waters of the Pagsanjan River possess high kinetic energy, allowing them to carve through rocks.
The Philippines has large magnetite sand deposits in Cagayan, which are naturally magnetic iron ores.
The Malampaya natural gas platform off Palawan generates electricity by burning gas to spin massive turbines.
The translucent shells of the windowpane oyster (Placuna placenta) are used in traditional lamps to softly diffuse light.
The giant bamboo batingaw of the Ibaloi people produces sound through vibrating air columns inside its tubes.
The hot springs of Mount Pulag transfer thermal heat from deep underground rocks to the surface water.
The geothermal power plant in Tiwi, Albay converts thermal energy from underground magma into electrical energy.
The zigzag portion of the Halsema Highway acts as an inclined plane to reduce the force needed to climb.
The wing-like patagium of the Philippine flying dragon (Draco mindanensis) reduces air resistance, allowing it to glide.
Gravity accelerates the falling waters of the Maria Cristina Falls to generate hydroelectric power in Mindanao.
